title: The Last Minute of the War
sub: Grades 5–8 · Social Studies · Reading the record of November 11, 1918
objective: Students will read the 1918 sound-ranging record, which shows the guns on one front firing until 11:00 AM on November 11, 1918, and silent after it, as a primary source. They will put the war’s numbers in scale, follow November 11 to **Armistice Day** (1919) and **Veterans Day** (1954), and practice **corroboration**: checking the record against the poster and the film, and judging what each can and cannot show.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: A strip of film, a poster and a film’s title card all tell of the same minute. Checking one against another is how historians decide what happened, and why a whole country still stops at 11 o’clock.

materials: The record, the numbers and the days on page 3, projected or printed
*When the Guns Fell Silent*, the exhibition’s short film, on a screen if you have one
connection: **Online,** play *When the Guns Fell Silent*: a countdown, six title cards and the record scrolling past, with the guns cut dead at 11:00. Then open *The Memorial* and keep the two minutes’ silence. **In the exhibition,** read the date and time in red on the poster, and take a soldier card from the display.

steps.title: A strip of film
script: Show the record without explaining it. *“Something changed in the middle of this strip. What, and when?”* Let students find the six lines, jagged then flat, the words *All guns firing* and *All guns silent*, and the time marks. Then tell them what it is: The Imperial War Museum describes it as a photograph of the record by sound ranging of artillery activity on the American front near the River Moselle, for one minute before and one minute after the Armistice at 11 AM on November 11, 1918.

All guns firing.”, then a blank gap, then flat on the right under “One minute after the hour. All guns silent.”, with time marks from 10.58-56 to 11.01-03 beneath
screen.caption: “The End of the War. A Graphic Record.”

steps.purpose: Look closely at a primary source before anyone explains it.
students: Something changed in the middle of this strip. What, and when?
What do the words on it tell you?

steps.title: The war in numbers
script: **The numbers (page 3).** Read them together and ask what each counts. America entered the war in April 1917 and two million young men crossed the Atlantic; over 116,000 American soldiers died, 53,000 in combat and another 63,000 from disease and accidents. Around 20 million people died in all, soldiers and civilians alike: *“the war to end all wars”* became one of the deadliest in history.

steps.purpose: Put the war in scale, and see what each number counts.
students: Why might a museum give both 116,000 and 20 million?

steps.title: The last morning
script: **The last morning.** The armistice was known to take effect at 11:00 AM, yet some commanders still ordered attacks that morning. Nearly 11,000 soldiers became casualties on November 11 alone. Canadian Private George Lawrence Price was shot at 10:58 AM; a minute later, Private Henry Gunther became the last American to die. Then point to the record: until 11:00, *all guns firing*.

screen.cite: When the Guns Fell Silent at the 11th Hour

steps.purpose: See that the war went on until the very last minute.
students: The war would end at 11:00. Why did the fighting not stop sooner?
What does the record show at 10:59?

steps.title: From Armistice Day to Veterans Day
script: **The day after.** In 1919 President Woodrow Wilson proclaimed *Armistice Day*, and Americans paused for two minutes at 11:00 AM. In 1954, after World War II and the Korean War, Congress renamed it *Veterans Day*, to honor all American veterans. Canada, Britain and France still call it *Remembrance Day*.

screen.caption: From the armistice to Veterans Day, as the When the Guns Fell Silent poster tells it

cells: At 11:00 AM the armistice, the peace agreement, takes effect. Church bells ring across Europe.
President Woodrow Wilson proclaims Armistice Day, “filled with solemn pride in the heroism of those who died in the country’s service.” At 11:00 AM Americans pause their work for two minutes.
After World War II and the Korean War, Congress changes the name to Veterans Day, to honor all American veterans, not just those from World War I.
Canada, Britain and France still call it Remembrance Day, and keep the two-minute silence at the eleventh hour. At Arlington, a wreath is placed at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.

steps.purpose: Follow November 11 from the end of the war to today.
students: Who made Armistice Day, and who renamed it?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout; all three work from the same sources.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Read the record closely and say what it shows. Match each number to what it counts. Put five dates from 1917 to 1954 in order.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Source the record: who, what, when, where, and what it cannot tell. Compare it with the poster’s account of the last hour, and explain why Armistice Day became Veterans Day.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Corroborate three accounts of the last minutes: the record, the poster and the film. Weigh what one strip of film from one front can prove, then argue why the war is still remembered.

steps.purpose: Work from the same sources at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three read the record, the numbers and the story of November 11.

steps.title: Three sources, one minute
script: Set the three accounts side by side. They agree: the guns fired until 11:00, and the last soldiers fell in the minutes before. The record shows the moment on one front; the poster names the last men.

screen.text:
The record · “One minute after the hour. All guns silent.”
The poster · Price at 10:58 AM; “a minute later,” Gunther
The film · “After one final soldier fell at 10:59 AM.”
screen.cite: The record, the poster and the film

steps.purpose: Set the three accounts side by side and ask whether they agree.
students: Do the three sources agree? Where?
What can the record show that the poster cannot, and the other way round?

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the objectives back on the screen, asked as questions: *“Can you now…?”* Students show a thumb up, sideways or down; for the last, ask a Red Level reader.
